note: The V/F work, 27 Aug 2026. Two separable results: (1) the shipped alpha-power fit was UNPHYSICAL and is corrected, and (2) a MEASURED product curve now exists and it carries temperature, which no other V/F source in this repository does. Neither changes any historical result -- nothing in the solve path uses the alpha fit, and the product curve is new. Both change what can be claimed next.

1_the_alpha_fit_was_outside_its_own_mode.defect: performance_model.VF_ALPHA_POWER_FIT had alpha = 0.949. Gonzalez, Gordon & Horowitz (JSSC 32(8), 1997) bound alpha between 1 (complete velocity saturation) and 2 (none). f(V) = k(V-Vth)^alpha/V has an interior maximum at Vth/(1-alpha) ONLY when alpha < 1, which is where the reported 6.43 GHz ceiling at 9.40 V came from -- an artefact of the exponent, not a property of any device.
1_the_alpha_fit_was_outside_its_own_mode.the_bound_binds: The constrained fit lands EXACTLY on alpha = 1.0 and its error rises from 0.28% to 0.74% RMS. Meanwhile the textbook's typical 1.4 misfits by 4.93% RMS -- seventeen times worse than the free fit.
1_the_alpha_fit_was_outside_its_own_mode.what_that_actually_means: The honest conclusion is not 'we had the wrong exponent' but 'the alpha-power law is the wrong model for this table'. The data actively resist the physical range. Look at the shape: 1.5 GHz per 200 mV at the bottom (0.6-0.8 V), 0.1 GHz per ~50 mV at the top (above 1.19 V). A single device's delay law does not saturate like that; a PRODUCT BIN TABLE does, because the top of the range is reliability-limited guardbanding. This is the clearest evidence in the repository that VF_PAIRS is a binning artefact rather than a device curve -- and therefore why a defensible product curve needs product data, not a better fit.

superseded_alpha_0949.6.5: unreachable at any voltage -- an ARTEFACT of the turnover

1_the_alpha_fit_was_outside_its_own_mode.what_does_NOT_change: The 5.0 GHz table top is still a DEVICE limit at 1.4 V, not a truncated lookup: the corrected curve needs 1.71 V for 5.5 GHz and 2.26 V for 6.0. A vf_clamped verdict stays a result -- voltage-limited, not thermally limited. And nothing in the solve path uses either fit (only frequency_for_voltage and voltage_for_frequency_extrapolated do), so no historical number moves.
1_the_alpha_fit_was_outside_its_own_mode.blast_radius: none; two reporting functions only. Verified by grep across the repository.

2_a_measured_product_curve_that_carries_.what_it_is: Measurements of AMD's own SMU V/F curve through Curve Optimizer and Curve Shaper. Curve Shaper exposes 15 tuning points -- 5 frequency regions x 3 temperature points (-5, 50, 90 C) -- which is itself the finding that a real product V/F curve is a SURFACE over (f, T), not a line.
2_a_measured_product_curve_that_carries_.what_it_is_not: A datasheet. This is enthusiast-press measurement of ONE part, and product V/F curves are per-part: each die is calibrated at test and its curve fused. That is why no vendor publishes a frequency->voltage table -- Intel's published VID tables are an 8-bit code->volts ENCODING, not a frequency mapping. calibrated = False, for a different reason than IRDSVFModel: that is a projection nobody measured, this is a measurement with a sample size of one.

THE_LEVER_THIS_ADDS.claim: Cooling buys VOLTAGE, not only thermal headroom -- and the sensitivity grows steeply with frequency, roughly doubling between 4.77 and 5.17 GHz. Every clock result in this project so far was computed on a temperature-INDEPENDENT V/F curve, so this lever has been absent by construction: the same shape of omission as the unsourced dt_max = 10 K ceiling.
THE_LEVER_THIS_ADDS.honest_size: Modest but real and MEASURED: ~8% dynamic power at constant 5.165 GHz, or ~93 MHz (+1.7%) at a fixed 1.35 V ceiling, for a 50 K reduction. It is wholly independent of the runaway/cliff mechanism, so it ADDS to the packaging and laser terms rather than overlapping them.
THE_LEVER_THIS_ADDS.conservatism: dV/dT is held FLAT outside the two measured frequencies rather than extrapolated. The trend is steeply increasing, so extending it would overstate the LCMR benefit; holding it flat makes the error run the safe way.

against_the_shipped_table.and: the shipped table calls 1.4 V / 5.0 GHz the device limit, while a shipping part reaches 5.63 GHz at 1.35 V. The table's ceiling is a property of the table.

consequence_for_the_ladder: 'Does LCMR reach 6 GHz?' was answered NO on every curve available, for a non-thermal reason. That answer was computed on the shipped table (5.0 GHz at 1.4 V) and on IRDS projections (3.34-4.54 GHz), both of which are now known to be well below what ships: a measured Zen 5 part does 5.63 GHz at 1.35 V, and 5.83 with an optimised curve. 6 GHz is far closer than either source suggested. This does NOT overturn the answer -- the measured curve stops at 5.63 GHz and must not be extrapolated -- but it removes the basis for the confident no, and it means the question should be re-asked against product data rather than settled.
